title: The Four Pillars Of Personal Finance
summary: Assets, liabilities, income and expenses explained with Indian examples, plus a worked net-worth sheet and a monthly cash-flow line you can copy.
body_markdown:
The four pillars of personal finance are usually given as assets, liabilities, income and expenses. In plain words: what you own, what you owe, what comes in and what goes out. Look at all four together and you can see your net worth, and how much is left each month after expenses.


Net worth is the total value of your assets minus everything you owe. The rest of this page defines each pillar with Indian examples, then works through one invented person's numbers.


## What are the four pillars of personal finance?


The four pillars are assets, liabilities, income and expenses. They are one common way to sort your money, not an official list. No regulator defines "the pillars" of personal finance, and writers list three, four, five or seven areas.


Personal finance is how you earn, spend, save, borrow, invest and protect money over your life. Saving and investing build assets. Borrowing creates liabilities. Earning is income, and spending is expenses.


Some writers call these four the "core four". That phrase has no official meaning and different writers use it differently, so treat it as a label, not a rule.


## What counts as an asset?


An asset is something you own that has money value. Your bank balance, a mutual fund, your EPF account, a flat, jewellery and a scooter all qualify. It helps to sort assets by what they let you do with the money.


**Cash and deposits.** Your savings account and fixed deposits (FDs) sit here. An FD is money placed with a bank or company for a set period at a rate fixed when you open it. Interest is what the bank pays you for keeping money with it. The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) insures deposits such as savings, fixed, current and recurring deposits. The cover is up to ₹5,00,000 per depositor per bank, principal and interest together.


**Investments.** A mutual fund is a trust registered with SEBI. Each unit you own is a slice of everything the fund holds, so its value rises and falls with the market. No one can promise you a fixed return. When you sell units, the money arrives within 3 working days from the date of redemption.


**Money you own but cannot spend freely.** Your Employees' Provident Fund (EPF) balance is yours, but it can be withdrawn only under the EPF withdrawal rules. A Public Provident Fund (PPF) account may be closed after 15 years from the end of the year in which it was opened. Partial withdrawal is allowed from the 7th financial year. Both count as assets. Neither is spending money. Our guide to[PF withdrawal rules](https://koshex.com/blog/pf-withdrawal-rules-a-comprehensive-guide-to-rules-documents-required-and-types) covers the EPF side, and the[PPF account guide](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-open-a-ppf-account) covers PPF.


**Things you use.** A two-wheeler or gold jewellery has money value, but the figure is an estimate until you sell. Gold's price also moves: in RBI's yearly averages since 1985-86, gold's average price was lower than the year before in 8 years.


Money is liquid when you can turn it into cash quickly without losing value. A savings account balance is liquid. EPF and PPF balances are not, because their rules decide when the money can come out.


## What counts as a liability?


A liability is any money you owe. A loan is the common case: a home loan, an education loan, a vehicle loan or a personal loan. An unpaid credit-card bill is a liability too, and so is money borrowed from family.


Loans come in two broad kinds. A secured loan is backed by something you own, such as a home loan backed by the house. An unsecured loan, such as a personal loan or a card balance, has no such backing.


A loan such as a home loan is repaid through EMIs. An EMI (equated monthly instalment) is the fixed amount paid each month that covers interest and part of the loan. On a loan, interest is what the lender charges for the money you borrow. Our page on[how EMIs work](https://koshex.com/blog/what-are-emis-and-how-do-they-work) explains the mechanics. For this pillar, the question is how much you owe today. If a loan feels heavy,[5 steps to get out of a debt trap](https://koshex.com/blog/5-steps-to-get-out-of-a-debt-trap) is the place to go. For a home loan specifically, there is a separate look at whether to[prepay it or invest](https://koshex.com/blog/prepay-home-loan-or-invest) .


## What counts as income?


Income is money coming in. It comes from work, such as a salary, a business or freelance fees. It also comes from what you own: interest, rent and dividends.


Bank FD interest is taxed as "Income from other sources" at your slab rate, the same rates that apply to your salary. A dividend is cash a company pays its shareholders out of its profits. IDCW means payouts a fund makes from its income or gains, which reduce its NAV by the amount paid. NAV is the price of one unit of a fund. The[growth vs IDCW](https://koshex.com/blog/growth-vs-idcw) page compares the two options.


Gross pay is what you earn before deductions. Take-home pay is what reaches your bank after deductions such as TDS (tax deducted at source) and EPF. For the cash-flow line below, use take-home, because that is the money you can actually spend.


## What counts as an expense?


An expense is money going out. Fixed expenses stay about the same each month: rent, EMIs, a phone plan and other regular bills. Variable expenses change: food, travel, eating out.


A medical emergency is an unplanned expense, not a luxury. That is what emergency money is for. It is a separate pot kept for sudden costs, and[where to keep your emergency savings](https://koshex.com/blog/where-should-you-keep-your-emergency-savings) looks at it in detail.


One common budgeting rule of thumb is 50:30:20: about half of take-home pay for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for saving and investing. It is a rule of thumb, not a regulation. The[50-30-20 rule](https://koshex.com/blog/50-30-20-rule) page explains it, and[the ultimate guide to money management](https://koshex.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-money-management) covers budgeting as a whole.


## How do you work out your net worth?


Add up the value of everything you own, then subtract everything you owe. That is your net worth.


Take Kavya, 31, a software tester in Chandigarh. She is single and rents a flat. All the amounts below are invented for the example.


Assets Amount Liabilities Amount


Savings account ₹85,000 Education loan outstanding ₹3,10,000


Fixed deposit ₹1,50,000 Credit-card bill due ₹42,000


Mutual funds (current value) ₹2,60,000 Two-wheeler loan outstanding ₹55,000


EPF balance ₹3,90,000


Gold jewellery (rough resale value) ₹1,20,000


**Total assets** **₹10,05,000** **Total liabilities** **₹4,07,000**


Her net worth is ₹10,05,000 minus ₹4,07,000, which is ₹5,98,000.


- ₹3,90,000 of her assets is EPF. It counts, but she cannot spend it freely.
- The jewellery figure is an estimate. A jeweller's offer on the day could differ.
- The mutual fund figure changes every day with the market.
- Only ₹85,000 is cash today.


Net worth is a snapshot of one day. It can also be negative. That happens when loans are larger than what you own, as it can be early in a career with a large education loan. That says where you stand today, not where you will end up.


Recalculating once a year is a sensible rhythm. The[April checklist](https://koshex.com/blog/things-to-do-at-the-start-of-the-financial-year) is a natural moment to do it.


## How do the four pillars help you manage money?


Net worth tells you where you stand. Income minus expenses tells you how fast that can change.


Kavya's take-home pay is ₹58,000 a month. Her fixed expenses come to ₹31,500 and her variable expenses to ₹14,000. So ₹58,000 minus ₹31,500 minus ₹14,000 leaves ₹12,500. That leftover is her monthly cash flow.


What happens to the ₹12,500 is the job of a written plan. The guide to[financial planning for beginners](https://koshex.com/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-financial-planning-for-beginners) shows how to make one, and[investment planning](https://koshex.com/blog/what-is-investment-planning-and-why-is-it-important) picks up from there.


Each pillar has its own lever:


- **Income:** a raise, a new job or side work moves it up.
- **Expenses:** fixed costs such as rent weigh more than small cuts, as[ways to save money](https://koshex.com/blog/10-best-ways-to-save-money) explains.
- **Liabilities:** the balance shrinks as you repay, and[getting out of debt](https://koshex.com/blog/5-steps-to-get-out-of-a-debt-trap) covers that.
- **Assets:** saving and investing add to them. The difference between the two is in[savings vs investments](https://koshex.com/blog/difference-between-savings-and-investments) .


The pillars are a way of seeing, not a score. Fill in your own four lines, and the rest of your money decisions have somewhere to start from.
